theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is an operational budget?
options: A plan of expected income and running costs for a period
A list of the firm's buildings, vehicles and equipment
A report of the actual profit made in the last year
A daily record of the balance in the bank account

questions.stem: Which item belongs in the capital budget rather than the operating budget?
options: Cleaning supplies bought each month
A new air-conditioning plant for the building
Overtime paid to staff over the holidays
Telephone and internet charges for the whole year

questions.stem: Why does a firm set a timetable for preparing its budget?
options: To hold back decisions until the year has started
To let each manager choose their own deadline
So each stage is done in time for approval

questions.stem: Andre Morrison is preparing his department's budget for next year. What should it be based on first?
options: Last year's figures with 10% added to every line
The amount he would personally like to spend
What the other departments are planning to spend

questions.stem: What is incremental budgeting?

Starting from zero and justifying every cost line
Setting each budget by the number of customers
Letting each team spend what it needs as it goes

questions.stem: Managers at a hotel in Ocho Rios suspect that old costs are carried forward each year without question. Which approach helps most?
options: Incremental budgeting

questions.stem: Which budget adjusts its cost allowances to the actual level of activity?
options: A fixed budget
A capital budget

questions.stem: Which is the most reliable starting point for next year's expense budget?

Figures taken from a firm in a different industry

questions.stem: Why should the person preparing a budget write down the key assumptions?

So that the budget runs to more pages and looks thorough

To hide extra profit from the head office

Cut every single line by exactly 8% without further thought

questions.stem: What should a manager do with the budget once it is approved?
options: File it away safely until the same time next year comes round

questions.stem: What is a rolling budget?

options: To make the budget file look thick, complete and well prepared

To show other firms how the budget was built

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the budgeting method called in which every cost must be justified from nothing each year? (Two words, often hyphenated.)
What type of cost stays the same in total, whatever the level of output, in the short term?
What type of cost changes in total in direct line with output?
A café plans to sell 1,200 lunches a month at J$900 each. What is its monthly lunch income budget, in J$?
Labour was budgeted at J$300,000 but actually cost J$330,000. What one-word term is used in budget reports for the J$30,000 gap?
Actual costs are higher than budget. Is this variance favourable or adverse?
What is a small amount added to a budget for likely but uncertain extra costs called?
Supplies cost J$800,000 this year. A 5% price rise is expected for the same volume. What should next year's budget be, in J$?
What is the name for the overall budget that brings together all the departmental and functional budgets? (Two words.)
What is the title given to the manager responsible for a budget line or cost centre? (Two words.)
A yearly rent budget of J$2,400,000 is phased equally. What is the monthly figure, in J$?
What is spending on long-lasting assets such as buildings and machinery called? (Two words.)
What is the term for the one resource (such as machine time or skilled staff) that limits how much a firm can produce? (Two words.)
A department's budget is J$5,000,000 and staff costs are J$3,250,000 of it. What percentage of the budget is staff cost?
What is the usual name for the twelve-month period that a budget covers? (Two words.)

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you would prepare next year's operating budget for your department.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by getting the budget timetable, guidelines and templates from finance, and the organisation's goals for the year, so the budget supports the plan. Next, I would gather data: last year's actual income and costs by month, this year's figures to date, and known changes such as new services, staff changes, contracts or price rises. With my team leaders, I would agree the expected level of activity, for example the number of clients or units, since many costs depend on it. I would then build the income budget, followed by the cost lines, separating fixed and variable costs and working out staff costs with statutory contributions and overtime. Each line would be phased by month to match the pattern of the year, and a small contingency added if allowed. I would write down every assumption, such as prices, exchange rates and volumes, and test what happens if the main ones change. After checking all formulas and totals, and asking a colleague to review it, I would submit the draft with a short explanation, and then revise it after discussion with senior management.
markingPoints: Obtains timetable, guidelines and organisational goals first
Gathers historical data and known changes; agrees activity levels with team leaders
Builds income then costs, separating fixed and variable, including full staff costs
Phases by month, adds contingency, records and tests assumptions
Checks, gets a second review, submits with explanation and revises after discussion

essays.stem: Compare incremental and zero-based budgeting. Recommend which a public agency should use for a department whose costs have grown for years without review.
essays.modelAnswer: Incremental budgeting takes last year's budget or actual figures as the base and adds or subtracts amounts for known changes, such as inflation or a new post. It is quick, simple and stable, and suits areas where activity changes little from year to year. Its weakness is that it accepts the base without question, so waste and out-of-date spending are carried forward year after year, and managers may spend everything to protect next year's budget. Zero-based budgeting starts each line from zero. Each activity must be justified by what it achieves and costed from scratch, and activities are ranked so that funds go to the most important first. This exposes waste and links spending to priorities, but it takes much more time, skill and data, and can cause anxiety among staff. For a department whose costs have grown for years without review, I recommend zero-based budgeting, at least for one cycle, because the problem is the untested base. The agency should give managers training and enough time, and may then return to incremental budgeting with regular reviews.
markingPoints: Explains incremental budgeting and its strengths (quick, simple, stable)
Weaknesses of incremental: carries waste forward, 'spend it or lose it'
Explains zero-based budgeting: justify every activity from zero, rank priorities
Weighs zero-based costs (time, skill, data, anxiety) against benefits
Recommends zero-based for this department with justification and support

essays.stem: A small bakery plans to make 8,000 loaves a month next year. Ingredients cost J$120 a loaf, packaging J$15 a loaf, and fixed costs are J$600,000 a month. Calculate the monthly variable costs and total costs, and explain how the budget would change if output rose to 9,000 loaves.
essays.modelAnswer: The variable cost per loaf is ingredients plus packaging: J$120 plus J$15 equals J$135. At 8,000 loaves, the monthly variable cost is 8,000 times J$135, which is J$1,080,000. Adding the fixed costs of J$600,000 gives a total monthly cost budget of J$1,680,000. If output rose to 9,000 loaves, the variable cost would rise to 9,000 times J$135, which is J$1,215,000, an increase of J$135,000. The fixed costs would stay at J$600,000, provided the bakery has the oven capacity and staff to make the extra loaves without new equipment or extra shifts. The total cost would then be J$1,815,000. The cost per loaf would fall, from J$210 at 8,000 loaves to about J$201.67 at 9,000, because the fixed cost is spread over more loaves. This shows why the budget should separate fixed and variable costs: it lets the manager flex the budget to the real level of output and see the effect of growth on costs and on profit.
markingPoints: Variable cost per loaf J$135; monthly variable cost J$1,080,000
Total monthly cost J$1,680,000
At 9,000 loaves: variable J$1,215,000, total J$1,815,000
Notes fixed costs stay the same only within capacity; cost per loaf falls (J$210 to about J$201.67)
Explains the value of separating fixed and variable costs (flexing the budget)

essays.stem: Explain why and how a manager should involve her team in preparing the operating budget.
essays.modelAnswer: Team members know the day-to-day work: how many jobs they handle, which equipment is wearing out, where waste happens and what supplies really cost. Involving them gives the manager better information, so the budget is more accurate. People who help build a budget are also more likely to accept it and work to keep within it, because they understand the targets and feel some ownership. Their ideas can reveal savings. However, the manager must keep control, as team members may ask for more than the organisation can afford. To involve them, she should explain the organisation's goals and any limits, such as a target to hold costs flat. She can ask team leaders to estimate activity and costs for their area, using a simple template and last year's figures, by a set date. A short meeting lets the team discuss priorities and trade-offs. The manager then combines the estimates, challenges any that look high or unsupported, and explains her final choices. Once the budget is approved, she shares it with the team and reports progress against it regularly.
markingPoints: Why: better information and accuracy from those who do the work
Why: ownership and commitment; ideas for savings
Keeps control; explains goals and limits up front
How: templates, data and deadlines; team meeting on priorities
Challenges estimates, explains final choices, shares the approved budget and reports progress

essays.stem: Explain the role of assumptions in an operating budget, and describe how a manager should record and test them.
essays.modelAnswer: Every budget is a forecast, so it rests on assumptions about the future: the level of activity, prices and wage rates, inflation, exchange rates, staffing, the timing of new services and customers' payment patterns. If an assumption is wrong, every figure that depends on it will be wrong too. The manager should list the key assumptions on a separate sheet at the front of the budget, with the source of each, for example 'supplier price rise of 6%, based on the supplier's letter' or 'US$ priced at the rate set by finance'. In a spreadsheet, each assumption should sit in its own input cell that formulas refer to, so it can be changed in one place. She should then test the most important assumptions by sensitivity analysis: what happens to the budget if sales fall by 10%, or the exchange rate moves by 5%? A best case and worst case can be prepared as well. This shows reviewers how robust the budget is, helps them approve it with their eyes open, and makes it easier to explain variances later when actual results come in.
markingPoints: Explains that the budget rests on assumptions and names typical ones
Records each key assumption with its source
Places assumptions in input cells linked to formulas
Tests key assumptions by sensitivity analysis or best/worst cases
Explains the benefit: reviewers understand risk and variances are easier to explain

essays.stem: Explain why a hotel's operating budget should be phased by month, and describe how you would phase its income and main costs.
essays.modelAnswer: A yearly total does not show when income and costs happen. Hotels in Jamaica have strong seasons: winter months and holidays are busy, while some months of the late summer and autumn are slower. If the budget is spread equally, managers cannot see whether a quiet month is normal or a warning sign, and the cash budget built from it will be wrong. To phase income, I would use the pattern of past years: work out each month's share of the year's room nights and average rates, adjust for known events such as festivals, conferences or a planned refurbishment, and apply these shares to the yearly income figure. Variable costs, such as food, laundry, guest supplies and commission, would follow the same pattern, since they move with occupancy. Staff costs would follow the planned rota, with extra casual staff and overtime in peak months. Fixed costs, such as insurance and rent, would be phased in the months they are paid or spread evenly if they accrue evenly. Utilities would follow both season and weather. The phased budget gives a fair monthly target to compare with actual results.
markingPoints: Explains why: seasonality, meaningful monthly comparison, accurate cash budget
Phases income using past seasonal patterns, adjusted for known events
Phases variable costs in line with occupancy
Phases staff costs by rota and fixed costs by payment pattern
Shows the phased budget gives fair monthly targets

essays.stem: Senior management asks you to cut your draft budget by 10%. Evaluate the ways you could respond, and recommend the best approach.
essays.modelAnswer: One response is to cut every line by 10%. This is quick and seems fair, but it ignores priorities: an essential line such as safety maintenance suffers as much as a line with waste in it. A second response is to refuse and defend the draft. This may be right if cuts would break the law or put people at risk, but on its own it damages the relationship and rarely succeeds. A third response is to cut whole activities, such as training or one service. This can find large savings but may cause hidden costs later. The best approach is a reasoned review. I would rank activities by how essential they are to the department's goals, look for savings in lower-priority lines first, and question any padding or contingency. I would look at other ways to meet the target, such as renegotiating supplier prices, changing timing or raising income. I would then present options to management showing the effect of each cut on service, risk and staff, and recommend a package that reaches 10% with the least harm, clearly stating any risks that remain.
markingPoints: Evaluates an equal cut on every line (quick but ignores priorities)
Evaluates refusing/defending (valid only for legal or safety needs)
Evaluates cutting whole activities (large savings, hidden costs)
Recommends a priority-based review including savings, timing and income
Presents options and their effects, with remaining risks stated

essays.stem: Describe how you would design a spreadsheet for an operating budget so that it is accurate and easy to review.
essays.modelAnswer: I would use separate sheets: one for assumptions and inputs, one or more for workings, and a summary sheet. The assumptions sheet holds every key input, such as volumes, prices, wage rates, exchange rate and inflation, each in a labelled cell with its source. Workings sheets calculate each line from those inputs by formula, never by typing numbers into formulas, so a change in an input flows through the whole budget. Each line would have its own row, with months in columns and a total column, and lines grouped under clear headings such as income, staff costs and operating costs, with subtotals. I would use the same layout and formulas across rows, and colour input cells differently from formula cells. Totals should be cross-checked, for example by adding across and down and making sure both match. Cells with formulas can be protected to avoid accidental changes. A notes column explains unusual figures. I would save versions with dates in the file name, keep a backup, and ask a colleague to test the sheet by changing an input and checking that the results move as expected.
markingPoints: Separate sheets for assumptions, workings and summary
Formulas link to labelled input cells; no hard-typed numbers in formulas
Clear layout: one row per line, months in columns, headings, subtotals and totals
Checks and protection: cross-totals, colour coding, protected cells, notes
Version control, backup and a test by a colleague

essays.stem: Explain how preparing an operating budget in a ministry or parish council differs from preparing one in a private firm.
essays.modelAnswer: In a private firm, the operating budget is driven mainly by expected sales and profit targets set by the owners or board. Income comes from customers, and if sales rise the firm can usually spend more to meet demand. Managers have some freedom to move funds between lines if senior management agrees. In a ministry or parish council, the budget is driven by the services it must provide and by the funds allocated through the government's budget process, along with any fees or local revenue it collects. The timetable is fixed by the central budget calendar, and the budget must be prepared in the set format and classified by programme and type of spending. Spending must stay within the approved amounts, and funds usually cannot be moved between lines without proper approval. Accountability is to the public, through the responsible ministry, Parliament or council members and the auditors, so the budget must be justified by results for citizens and documented carefully. Purchases built into the budget must follow the procurement rules for public bodies. Both sectors need accurate data, assumptions and consultation, but the public sector has tighter rules and wider accountability.
markingPoints: Private firm: driven by sales and profit targets; more flexibility
Public body: driven by mandated services and allocated funds within a central budget process
Public body: fixed calendar, set formats, spending within approved amounts, limits on moving funds
Public accountability and audit; procurement rules apply
Notes common ground: data, assumptions, consultation

essays.stem: Justify why a manager should present and explain the approved budget to the team, and describe what she should cover.
essays.modelAnswer: A budget only works if the people who spend the money and earn the income understand it. If staff do not know the targets and limits, they cannot help to meet them, and overspending or missed income may only be noticed months later. Presenting the budget also shows openness, builds trust and invites ideas for saving money. In a short team session, the manager should first link the budget to the organisation's goals for the year, so staff see why the figures matter. She should explain the main income targets and cost limits for the team, highlight what has changed from last year and why, and point out any lines where savings are needed. Each budget holder should be told which lines they are responsible for and how much authority they have to spend. She should explain how and when actual results will be reported, for example a monthly report comparing actual with budget, and what to do if a cost is likely to go over. She should end by inviting questions and suggestions, and follow up in writing with the key figures.
markingPoints: Justifies: staff can only meet targets they understand; early warning of problems
Builds trust and invites ideas
Links the budget to goals and explains main targets, limits and changes
Names budget holders and their authority; explains reporting and what to do about overspends
Invites questions and follows up in writing

practical1.title: Prepare a draft operating budget for a department
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a data pack for one department of a made-up organisation (for example the housekeeping department of a 60-room hotel in St Ann, or the training unit of a public agency): last year's actual costs by month, planned activity for next year, known price changes and staffing. As a group, prepare a draft twelve-month operating budget in a spreadsheet. Give each member a named role: activity and income lead (volumes and any income), staff cost lead (salaries, overtime and employer contributions using only the figures given), operating cost lead (supplies, utilities and other costs, split into fixed and variable), spreadsheet and phasing lead (builds the layout and phases each line by month), and reviewer (keeps the assumptions sheet, tests one assumption by sensitivity, and checks every formula and total twice). In a group of four, the spreadsheet lead also does the review. Photograph or screenshot each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Computers with spreadsheet software and a printer
photos: The flipchart plan: roles, budget lines and the list of assumptions
The workings for staff costs and for fixed and variable costs
The phased twelve-month budget with totals
The sensitivity test (for example, activity 10% lower) on screen
checklist: Took a named role and prepared their lines of the budget
Used the data pack correctly, separating fixed and variable costs
Staff costs include the elements given, with no invented rates
Lines are phased sensibly by month and totals are correct, checked twice
Assumptions are written down with sources and placed in input cells
Sensitivity test shows the effect of a change in a key assumption
Layout is clear for a manager to review
safety: Use only the made-up data given; keep the draft confidential to the group and assessor
Save work to the Centre's folder and do not share login details
Share the workload fairly and agree realistic times for each part
Take short screen breaks and keep cables tidy

practical2.title: Revise and present a budget for approval
practical2.brief: Using the draft budget from Practical 1 (or a draft given by the assessor), your group must respond to a request from senior management to cut the total by 8% while protecting essential services. Hold a short planning meeting, then prepare: a revised budget showing each change, a one-page impact statement (what each cut will mean for service, staff and risk), and a flexible budget table showing total costs at 90%, 100% and 110% of planned activity. Present your revised budget to a panel (the assessor and members of another group) in 10 minutes, with slides, and answer questions. Give each member a named role: chair of the planning meeting, finance lead (works the 8% target and the flexible budget), impact writer, presenter, and note-taker (records decisions and the panel's questions). Every member must speak in the presentation or the questions. Photograph each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Draft budget from Practical 1 or from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and presentation software
photos: The planning meeting notes showing the priority ranking of budget lines
The revised budget on screen with changes marked and the new total
The flexible budget table at 90%, 100% and 110% activity
The group presenting to the panel
checklist: Took a named role and contributed to the planning meeting
Revised total meets the 8% cut, worked correctly and checked twice
Cuts are based on priorities, not an equal cut on every line, with reasons given
Flexible budget correctly separates fixed and variable costs at each activity level
Impact statement is clear and honest about service, staff and risk
Presented or answered questions clearly and respectfully
safety: Discuss staff costs in general terms only; never use real people's pay
Respect other members' views in the planning meeting
Keep projector and extension leads out of walkways
Keep the workload fair and take a short break between preparing and presenting
